title: All is burning, read whole

lines: A THOUSAND MEN ON GAYA HEAD.
cards: A thousand men sit on a hill near Gaya. Until recently, every one of them tended sacred fires.
They kept their hair matted and twisted, and poured offerings into flames morning and night, under three brothers named Kassapa. Now they've become monks, followers of the Buddha.
And the Buddha, standing on Gaya Head, gives them a sermon in a language they have lived inside for years. Fire. Year one told the story.
Today, the sermon itself, the way they heard it.

teach.h: WHAT IS THE ALL THAT IS BURNING?
teach.b: SN 35.28 opens: all is burning, monks. And what is the all that is burning? Then it walks through the senses, one by one, with a rhythm meant to be heard.
The eye is burning. Forms are burning. Eye-consciousness is burning.
And whatever feeling arises from eye-contact, pleasant, painful or neither, that too is burning. Burning with what?
With the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. Burning with birth, aging and death, with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair, I say.

Then again for the ear and sounds, the nose and smells, the tongue and tastes, the body and touch, the mind and ideas. Six times the same pattern, until the whole world of experience is on fire. Then the turn.
Seeing this, the well-taught disciple grows disenchanted with all of it.
Disenchanted, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are freed. And the text ends: while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of those thousand monks were freed from the taints.
What makes it work isn't a theory of fire. It's an image these men had lived inside for years. They knew how fire feeds on fuel and goes out when the fuel is gone.
Buddhist teachers hear the same picture in the word nibbana: a fire going out. And the sermon ends the way a fire does, when nothing is left to feed it.

how: The Adittapariyaya Sutta, the fire sermon, is studied and chanted in many Theravada communities, and its pattern of the six senses is a common frame for meditation on sense experience.

o: burning, on fire with lust and hate
the sun rising over the hilltop
a sacred fire tended with offerings

s: the fire sermon covers only the eye
it walks through all six senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind.
the monks who heard it had tended sacred fires
they were matted-hair fire ascetics under the three Kassapa brothers.
the thousand monks were freed while the sermon was still being spoken
the text says their minds were freed from the taints as they listened.

games.q: you're the Buddha, about to teach a thousand men who've spent their lives tending sacred fires. what image do you use?
games.why: he speaks in the language they know best: everything they experience is burning, and freedom is the fire going out.

practice: If you're somewhere you can, read the sermon's pattern softly aloud, or silently, at the pace of the breath: the eye is burning, forms are burning, the ear, sounds, the nose, smells, the tongue, tastes, the body, touch, the mind, ideas.
Let each line land in the sense it names: look, listen, smell, taste, feel, think. Then sit quietly with whatever is left after the words stop.

wordCard.voice: Aditta. The Pali word for burning, in the fire sermon of SN 35.28: the six senses, their objects and feelings, burning with lust, hatred and delusion, cooled by letting go. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali aditta: burning, on fire. SN 35.28 is the Adittapariyaya Sutta, the discourse on burning.

carryVoice: Your line: a little less fuel. Lust, hatred and delusion burn on what they're fed. Day six hundred fifty-two.
